page: Vultr voc-s-16c-128gb-3840s-amd is an instance in the Optimized Cloud Compute family, configured with dedicated AMD EPYC processors running at a base clock of 2.0 GHz. Built on the x86_64 architecture, the instance provides 16 virtual CPUs backed by 8 physical cores with simultaneous multithreading. Memory allocation is generous at 128 GB of RAM, yielding an 8:1 memory-to-vCPU ratio. Attached storage consists of a bundled 3840 GB local NVMe SSD, and networking includes one complimentary public IPv4 address without discrete GPU acceleration.

Benchmark measurements indicate solid compute capability, led by a strong single-core stress-ng result in the top quartile of tested instances. Multi-threaded throughput aligns with the median baseline, reflected in a Geekbench multi-core score of 10847.0 and a PassMark CPU score of 31969.29. Uncached memory bandwidth reaches 123.94 GB/s for reads and 70.41 GB/s for writes. Storage-adjacent throughput demonstrates solid operational rates, achieving 28.04 million Redis SET operations per second and 15.37 GB/s in static web serving benchmarks.

The combination of high memory capacity and large local NVMe storage yields balanced resource density for stateful, I/O-intensive services. Because the instance pairs dedicated AMD cores with extensive memory rather than shared execution threads, resource contention remains minimal. It is well matched for mid-tier relational databases, in-memory caching tiers, large-scale Redis deployments, search indexing clusters, and high-throughput web backends.
description: Vultr voc-s-16c-128gb-3840s-amd is a memory-dense virtual machine within the Optimized Cloud Compute family. It features 16 dedicated vCPUs mapped across 8 AMD EPYC physical cores operating at 2.0 GHz on x86_64 architecture. The server is configured with 128 GB of system memory, providing an 8:1 memory-to-vCPU ratio suitable for memory-intensive architectures. Local storage is addressed by a bundled 3840 GB NVMe SSD, complemented by one public IPv4 address, with no hardware GPU acceleration. In synthetic testing, single-core CPU throughput performs in the top quartile, while multi-core metrics and uncached memory bandwidth show solid median results. The substantial local NVMe storage and dedicated hardware allocation make this configuration effective for production database hosting, in-memory data structures, caching layers, and search indexing workloads.
